text: Each lesson in this chapter looked at one layer on its own — identity, workload policy, control plane. A real pre-production review checks all of them together, because a gap in one undermines the others. Airtight RBAC doesn't help if a Pod can still run as root and escalate from inside the cluster, and a hardened API server doesn't help if cluster-admin is bound to a ServiceAccount nobody remembers creating. Work through this namespace by namespace, not once at the cluster level.

Start with RBAC. Query every ClusterRoleBinding tied to cluster-admin, and every name that comes back should be a human admin account you can justify, never a leftover ServiceAccount. Then spot-check workload identities directly with kubectl auth can-i --list, because reading Role and RoleBinding YAML can miss how multiple bindings combine — asking the real authorizer shows the actual effective permissions.

Next, confirm Pod Security Standards are actually enforced, not just assumed — pull every namespace's enforce label and treat a missing one as running on whatever the cluster default happens to be. Then check networking: Kubernetes allows all Pod-to-Pod traffic by default, so every workload namespace needs an explicit default-deny ingress policy, with real allows layered on top only for what needs to talk to what.

Confirm Secrets are actually encrypted, not just configured to be — enabling EncryptionConfiguration only protects writes going forward, so existing Secrets need a one-time rewrite to land through the new provider. Confirm etcd's ports are unreachable outside the control plane, and that a recent, encrypted backup has actually been test-restored at least once. Then confirm audit logging is on, rotated, and shipped somewhere a human or alert pipeline actually reads it.

Carry forward what earlier chapters already covered: images scanned in CI, running as non-root, referenced by digest rather than a mutable tag. Confirm resource requests and limits are set everywhere a ResourceQuota or LimitRange should be catching gaps. Confirm every public Ingress terminates real TLS, not plaintext.

Finally, run kube-bench against the cluster — an open-source tool from Aqua Security that checks control-plane and node configuration against the published CIS Kubernetes Benchmark. Treat it as a second opinion, not a replacement for the checks before it, and keep the result as a reproducible record for the next review. That closes out Chapter 7 — next, the capstone puts every object, network rule, and security control from this course to work on one real multi-service application.
